sections.title: Degree-Based Turns (Angle-Based Direction)
sections.content: Now, questions include angles like 90°, 45°, and 135°. 90° means a right angle turn. 180° means completely turning back (a U-turn). 135° means 90° + 45°. If a person is facing North and turns 135° clockwise, they will face the South-East direction.  Understand angles as parts of a full 360° rotation.

sections.title: Understanding Clockwise and Anti-clockwise
sections.content: Clockwise means moving in the direction of the clock's hands (North to East, East to South). Anti-clockwise means moving in the opposite direction of the clock (North to West). 45° represents the half angle between a main cardinal direction and a diagonal direction.

sections.title: Concept of Shadows
sections.content: In the morning, the sun is in the East, so the shadow falls towards the West. In the evening, the sun is in the West, so the shadow falls towards the East. [Image illustrating morning and evening shadow directions in logical reasoning] If the shadow is on the right side in the morning, the person's face will be towards the North. The actual direction is deduced based on the position of the sun.

sections.title: Relative Positioning
sections.content: If City A is North-East of City B, then A will be above and to the right of B. If City C is South of A and East of B, it is essential to draw a diagram combining the positions of all three. Always determine the first reference point and place the other locations sequentially.

sections.title: Clock-Based Direction Logic
sections.content: The 12 hours on a clock represent 360°. The distance from 12 to 3 is 90°.  If the minute hand is pointing North-East at 4:30, set the 12 position in that same direction. Then find the position of the hour hand at 9:15. Determine the direction by converting the time into angles.

sections.title: 3-4 Step Solution Strategy
sections.content: Step 1: Determine the starting direction. Step 2: Apply the given angles or turns. Step 3: Adjust the distance or position. Step 4: Find the final direction or shortest distance. Drawing a sequential, step-by-step diagram is helpful in every question.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Adding 135° in the wrong direction. 2. Forgetting the sun's direction in the morning vs. evening. 3. Messing up the sequence in Relative Positioning. 4. Forgetting the 30° per hour rule in clock questions.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 incorporates angles, sun position, relative locations, and clock-based logic along with basic direction. Step-by-step solving and clean diagrams are the keys to success.

tricks.title: Remember the 360° Rule
tricks.explanation: A full rotation is 360°. 90° = changing one direction, 180° = turning back.
tricks.example: Turning 180° from North leads to South.

tricks.title: Morning Shadow Trick
tricks.explanation: Morning sun is in the East, shadow is in the West.
tricks.example: If the morning shadow is on the right, the face is towards the North.

tricks.title: Evening Shadow Trick
tricks.explanation: Evening sun is in the West, shadow is in the East.
tricks.example: If the evening shadow is behind you, your face is towards the West.

tricks.title: Choose a Base Point in Relative Position
tricks.explanation: Make one city the center first, then place the rest.
tricks.example: Make B the center and place A in the North-East.

tricks.title: 30° Per Hour in a Clock
tricks.explanation: The hour hand moves 30° every hour.

tricks.title: Calculate Net Angle
tricks.explanation: Subtract the Clockwise and Anti-clockwise values.

tricks.title: Identify Diagonal Directions
tricks.explanation: North-East, South-East, etc., are at a 45° difference from main directions.

tricks.title: Step Diagram Method
tricks.explanation: Draw a new arrow after every single turn.
tricks.example: In a three-turn question, change the direction of your line three times.
